pairs.old: This page collects how the papers in the map define three terms: *faithfulness*, *counterfactual* and *monitorability*.
pairs.new: This site maps research on chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness and monitorability, and "the map" means its collection of papers. This page collects how the papers in the map define three terms: *faithfulness*, *counterfactual* and *monitorability*.

pairs.old: It rests on 3,414 definitions quoted from 216 of the 217 entries the map held when the catalogue was built.
pairs.new: It is based on 3,414 definitions quoted from 216 of the 217 papers that the map held when this collection of definitions was built.

pairs.old: The formal-framework papers added on 1 November 2026 have their own catalogue, in the Formal tab and on the [formal frameworks page](page.html?doc=formal).
pairs.new: The papers on formal frameworks that were added to the map on 1 November 2026 have their own collection of definitions, in the Formal tab of the dashboard and on the [formal frameworks page](page.html?doc=formal).

pairs.old: Each definition is quoted verbatim with its location in the paper, its kind (informal, formal, operational, criterion, failure mode or taxonomy) and its stance: proposed by the paper, or adopted or adapted from earlier work, in which case the row names the source (1,224 of the 1,225 borrowed rows do).
The full set is [`definitions.csv`](https://github.com/Dundalia/faithfulness-review/blob/main/definitions.csv), one row per definition, and the Definitions tab of the dashboard filters it.
pairs.new: The full set is in [`definitions.csv`](https://github.com/Dundalia/faithfulness-review/blob/main/definitions.csv), a table with one row per definition, and the Definitions tab of the dashboard lets you filter it.

pairs.old: For each term, the definitions are grouped into clusters of meaning.
pairs.new: For each term, the definitions are sorted into groups by meaning: a group collects definitions with a similar meaning.

pairs.old: Each section then traces who borrows which definition from whom, checks the borrowed definitions against their sources, and lists the points on which papers disagree.
pairs.new: Each term's section then traces which papers borrow which definition from which earlier papers, checks the borrowed definitions against their sources, and lists the points on which papers disagree.

pairs.old: In the tables, text in quotation marks is copied from the paper and text without quotation marks is a gloss.
pairs.new: In the tables, text in quotation marks is copied from the paper. Text without quotation marks is a short paraphrase, not a quote.

pairs.old: **Faithfulness has one common definition and nine relations that papers test, and the relations can disagree.**
pairs.new: **Faithfulness has one common definition and nine relations that papers test, and the relations can disagree.**

pairs.old: [Jacovi & Goldberg 2020](./#p=jacovi2020towards) define a faithful interpretation as one that "accurately represents the reasoning process behind the model’s prediction", and 79 rows from 55 papers cite them.
pairs.new: [Jacovi & Goldberg 2020](./#p=jacovi2020towards) define a faithful interpretation as one that "accurately represents the reasoning process behind the model’s prediction", and 79 definitions from 55 papers cite them.

pairs.old: Clusters 2 to 10 distinguish nine relations: what the trace discloses, whether the answer depends on the trace or agrees with it, whether an action matches what was said, whether the explanation lets an observer predict the model, whether a self-report matches the model's behavior or internal states, whether the marked inputs matter, whether the trace matches the internal computation, and whether a statement matches the model's belief.
pairs.new: Groups 2 to 10 of the faithfulness section distinguish nine relations. They ask what the trace discloses, whether the answer depends on the trace or agrees with it, whether an action matches what was said, and whether the explanation lets an observer predict the model. They also ask whether a self-report matches the model's behavior or internal states, whether the inputs that the explanation marks as important matter to the prediction, whether the trace matches the internal computation, and whether a statement matches the model's belief.

pairs.old: Some of them relax the common definition: [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) require that "$z$ is a sufficient statistic for $v$" for one property $v$, and [Viteri et al. 2024](./#p=viteri2026markovian) prioritize "informativeness over full faithfulness".
pairs.new: Some of these relations relax the common definition. [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) consider one property $v$ and require that "$z$ is a sufficient statistic for $v$", which means that $z$ (for example a CoT) contains all the information relevant to predicting $v$. [Viteri et al. 2024](./#p=viteri2026markovian) prioritize "informativeness over full faithfulness".

pairs.old: The relations can disagree on the same traces, and so can classifiers of a single relation: on identical data, the three hint-acknowledgment classifiers of [Young 2026a](./#p=young2026measuring) give overall faithfulness rates of 74.4%, 82.6% and 69.7%.
pairs.new: The relations can disagree on the same traces, and so can different classifiers of a single relation. In a hint test, a hint is inserted into the prompt, and a classifier decides whether the trace acknowledges it. On identical data, the three hint-acknowledgment classifiers of [Young 2026a](./#p=young2026measuring) give overall faithfulness rates of 74.4%, 82.6% and 69.7%.

pairs.old: **Counterfactual definitions differ on four points.**
pairs.new: **Counterfactual definitions differ on four points.**

pairs.old: They differ in what is varied, in whether the variant must change the output, in how a change in output becomes a causal claim, and in what the comparison judges: an explanation, the model's reliance on a feature, a self-report, a training target or a covert behavior.
pairs.new: They differ in what is changed to produce the variant (the counterfactual case), in whether the variant must change the model's output, in how a change in output is turned into a claim about cause, and in what the comparison of the original and the variant is used to judge: an explanation, the model's reliance on a feature, a self-report, a training target or a covert behavior.

pairs.old: The section on counterfactuals lists ten tensions that follow from these four points, among them whether the variant must change the output and whether one flipped answer shows that the edit caused it.
pairs.new: The section on counterfactuals lists ten points of disagreement that follow from these four differences. Among them are whether the variant must change the output, and whether one flipped answer (an answer that changes after an edit) shows that the edit caused it.

pairs.old: **Monitorability has two competing definitions, and they divide on faithfulness.**
pairs.new: **Monitorability has two competing definitions, and they disagree on whether, and how far, monitorability requires faithfulness.**

pairs.old: 42 rows from 24 papers make monitorability a monitor's ability to predict a property of the model's behavior, and 69 rows from 34 papers make it depend on the trace verbalizing what drove the answer; 9 papers have rows in both clusters.
pairs.new: In 42 definitions from 24 papers, monitorability is a monitor's ability to predict a property of the model's behavior. In 69 definitions from 34 papers, it depends on whether the trace verbalizes (states in words) what drove the answer. 9 papers have definitions in both groups.

pairs.old: [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) write that their notion "does not require a model’s externalized reasoning to faithfully reflect its internal reasoning process", and [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) require faithfulness only with respect to the monitored property.
pairs.new: [Guan et al. 2025](./#p=guan2025monitoring) write that their notion of monitorability "does not require a model’s externalized reasoning to faithfully reflect its internal reasoning process", and [Baker et al. 2025](./#p=baker2025monitoring) require faithfulness only with respect to the monitored property.

pairs.old: [Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness), [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) and [Anonymous 2026 (one draw)](./#p=anon2026one) state the requirement without that restriction.
pairs.new: [Jia et al. 2026](./#p=jia2026faithfulness), [Xiong et al. 2026](./#p=xiong2026monitorability) and [Anonymous 2026 (one draw)](./#p=anon2026one) state the faithfulness requirement without that restriction.

pairs.old: **82% of the checks find a borrowed definition in its cited source.**
pairs.new: **In 82% of the checks, the cited source contains the borrowed definition.**

pairs.old: Of the 804 borrowed rows that cite a source in the map, 803 have attribution checks, giving 1,095 row-source checks; the unchecked row is the cue-acknowledgment judge rubric of [Nguyen et al. 2026b](./#p=nguyen2026generalization), which cites [Meek et al. 2025](./#p=meek2025measuring).
pairs.new: Borrowed definitions were checked against the sources they cite, when those sources are in the map. Of the 804 borrowed definitions that cite a source in the map, 803 were checked. This gives 1,095 checks, one for each pair of a definition and a source in the map that it cites. The one unchecked definition is the rubric that [Nguyen et al. 2026b](./#p=nguyen2026generalization) give a judge model for cue acknowledgment (whether the model's reasoning or response mentions a cue inserted into the prompt); it cites [Meek et al. 2025](./#p=meek2025measuring).

pairs.old: 898 find the definition in the source, as stated (647) or adapted (251).
pairs.new: Each check ends in a verdict. In 898 checks, the source gives the definition, either as the paper states it (verdict "supported", 647 checks) or in a form that the citing paper modifies, for example by narrowing or extending it (verdict "adapted", 251 checks).

pairs.old: The other 197 are partial (122), renamed (43), support a different claim (13), are unsupported (15) or cite the wrong source (4).
pairs.new: The other 197 checks have one of five verdicts: "partial" (122), when the source supports only part of the definition; "renamed" (43), when the source defines the same thing under another name; "other-claim" (13), when the citation supports a claim other than the definition, such as a finding stated next to it; "unsupported" (15), when the source does not give the definition; and "misdirected" (4), when the definition comes from a different paper than the one cited.

pairs.old: The checks cover 803 of the 804 eligible rows, so these are rates for the catalogue, not for a sample.
pairs.new: The checks cover 803 of the 804 definitions that could be checked, so these are rates for the whole collection, not estimates from a sample.

pairs.new: Among the faithfulness definitions, ten checks find a source credited with a definition it does not give, and in three of them the source is [Jacovi & Goldberg 2020](./#p=jacovi2020towards).

pairs.old: **First extraction.** `scripts/definitions.py excerpt` kept each section of a paper's full text that mentions one of the terms, without the reference list and most appendices, and Claude agents quoted the definitions in those sections: 1,197 definitions.
pairs.new: **First collection of definitions, from excerpts.** A script (`scripts/definitions.py excerpt`) kept each section of a paper's full text that mentions one of the terms, leaving out the reference list and most appendices. Claude agents then quoted the definitions in those sections: 1,197 definitions.

pairs.old: The second pass showed that this missed definitions in methods sections and appendices.
pairs.new: The full reading in step 2 showed that this missed definitions in methods sections and appendices.

pairs.old: **Second pass over the full texts.** Agents read every paper in full, appendices included, and added, corrected or dropped rows.
pairs.new: **Second collection, from the full texts.** Agents read every paper in full, appendices included, and added, corrected or dropped definitions.

pairs.old: The scope was widened to honesty, say-do consistency and self-report accuracy (faithfulness) and to scheming, covert actions, sabotage, sandbagging, deception, reward hacking and verbalized evaluation awareness (monitorability).
pairs.new: The scope was also widened. For faithfulness, it now covers honesty, say-do consistency (whether a model's actions match what it said) and self-report accuracy (whether a model's reports about itself are true). For monitorability, it now covers scheming, covert actions, sabotage, sandbagging (deliberate underperformance), deception, reward hacking and verbalized evaluation awareness (a model saying in its reasoning that it may be under evaluation).

pairs.old: Pure introspection is out of scope, and so is faithfulness to a source document unless the paper contrasts it explicitly with the notions above: GPT-6.1 Sol (through Codex) screened the 130 rows that a keyword search flagged and dropped 20.
pairs.new: Pure introspection (a model's access to its own internal states, studied as a capability and not as the accuracy of its reports about itself) is out of scope. So is faithfulness to a source document (as in summarization), unless the paper explicitly contrasts it with the notions above. To apply these exclusions, another model, GPT-6.1 Sol (run through Codex), screened the 130 definitions that a keyword search flagged and dropped 20.

pairs.new: A check of a sample of 12 added definitions found 3 errors (one definition out of scope, and two with the wrong stance or source), and they are fixed (`checks/sample_audit_*.json`).

pairs.new: **Grouping the definitions and writing the sections.** For each term, one agent placed every definition in exactly one group (the `cluster` column of the CSV file) and wrote the term's section. It also listed each factual claim that the section makes: 607 claims in all.
